label: Chapter 7: Rebuilding and Founding Europe, 1945 to 1980

units.text: When the war ended, Luxembourg drew a conclusion that would shape the rest of its history: a small country cannot protect itself by standing alone.
Neutrality had been tried, and it had failed twice.
So the Grand Duchy did something that surprised many observers.
It threw itself into international cooperation, with an enthusiasm that few larger countries could match.
The process had begun even before the war ended.
In September 1944, while the exiled governments of Belgium, the Netherlands and Luxembourg were still sitting in London, they signed an agreement to create a customs union among the three countries.
The name for it was a combination of their initials: Benelux.
Fourteen years later, the three countries turned it into a full economic union.
In 1945, Luxembourg became a founding member of the United Nations.
In 1948, it formally rewrote its constitution to remove the clause that made it a perpetually neutral country.
And in 1949, it was one of the twelve founding members of NATO, the Western military alliance.
For a country with a tiny army, this was a bold declaration.
Luxembourg was now firmly part of the Western camp.
But the most important step was still to come, and the key figures in it had strong Luxembourg connections.
One was a man named Robert Schuman.
He was born in 1886 in Clausen, a neighborhood in Luxembourg City, to a mother from Luxembourg and a father from the French region of Lorraine.
He grew up speaking German and French and Luxembourgish, studied in Germany, and eventually became a French politician.
After the Second World War, he served as France's foreign minister.
On the ninth of May, 1950, Schuman made an announcement that changed the history of Europe.
He proposed that France and Germany, who had fought three wars in less than a century, should place their coal and steel production under a single common authority, open to other European countries.
The idea was that if the raw materials of war were jointly controlled, a new war between the two nations would become unthinkable.
This is known as the Schuman Declaration, and May ninth is celebrated today as Europe Day.
The result was the European Coal and Steel Community, set up by six countries in 1951: France, West Germany, Italy, Belgium, the Netherlands, and Luxembourg.
And Luxembourg was a natural participant.
It was one of Europe's biggest producers of steel per head of population.
Its steel company ARBED was one of the giants of the sector.
And its leaders had learned that tying themselves to bigger neighbors in a set of shared institutions was the best way to stay free.
Another leading figure was Joseph Bech, Luxembourg's foreign minister for more than thirty years, from 1926 to 1958.

In 1955, at a conference in the Sicilian town of Messina, Bech helped push forward a plan for a wider European common market, and that led to the Treaties of Rome in 1957, which created the European Economic Community,
the direct ancestor of today's European Union.
Luxembourg's government was small, but its diplomats were skilled, and they made themselves useful as mediators between France and Germany.
The country was rewarded. When the institutions of the new Europe were being placed, Luxembourg became one of their homes.
The High Authority of the Coal and Steel Community was based there from 1952.
So was the Court of Justice of the European Communities, which still sits in Luxembourg today as the Court of Justice of the European Union.
In 1968, the European Investment Bank, the EU's lending arm, set up its headquarters there.
In 1977, the European Court of Auditors followed.
Parts of the European Parliament's administration are in Luxembourg too, along with Eurostat, the EU's statistics office, and its publications office.
In a continent of far larger capitals, the little city on the Alzette had become, quietly, one of the capitals of Europe.
It also lent its name to a famous diplomatic fix.
In 1965, France's president Charles de Gaulle was furious about plans to give the European institutions more power, and he boycotted meetings for months, in what is known as the empty chair crisis.
The crisis was finally settled in January 1966 at a meeting in Luxembourg.
The deal is still known as the Luxembourg Compromise, and it effectively let a country block a decision if its vital national interests were at stake.
For decades afterwards, it shaped how Europe made decisions.
Meanwhile, back home, the country was rebuilding.
The north, devastated by the Battle of the Bulge, was rebuilt town by town.
Steel boomed in the postwar decades, as Europe needed girders, rails and machinery for reconstruction, and for years it was the largest single part of the economy.
Wages rose, new housing went up, and the standard of living climbed steadily.
On the throne, there was a change of generation.
Grand Duchess Charlotte, who had reigned for forty-five years and who had become the symbol of the country's survival, abdicated on the twelfth of November, 1964, in favor of her son, Jean.
Jean, who had fought alongside the Allies in the war, was forty-three, and he would reign for thirty-six years.
There was another, quieter change.
The steel mills needed workers, and Luxembourg's own population was too small to supply them.
Starting in the 1960s, thousands of people arrived from Portugal, escaping poverty and a dictatorship at home.
They worked in construction, in the steel mills, in hotels and restaurants.
Over the decades, they became the largest foreign community in the country, and today people of Portuguese origin make up about one in seven residents.
The Luxembourg of the postwar years was becoming a multicultural society, long before that was fashionable.
And then there was a financial first.
In 1963, an Italian motorway company raised money through a new kind of bond, sold outside its home country and denominated in a foreign currency.
It was the first so-called Eurobond, and it was listed on the Luxembourg stock exchange.
The reason Luxembourg got the business was simple: it was friendly, flexible, discreet, and had light regulation.
Over the next decade, banks from Germany, the United States, and elsewhere arrived to set up shop in the Grand Duchy.
This was the seed of a new economy.
One of the people who understood where all this was going was Pierre Werner, who was prime minister and finance minister for much of the 1960s and 1970s.
In 1970, European leaders asked a committee chaired by Werner to design a path toward a single European currency.
The result, the Werner Report, mapped out a step-by-step plan for economic and monetary union by 1980.
It was shelved after the monetary chaos of the early seventies and the oil crisis.
But its ideas came back twenty years later, and the euro, launched in 1999, owes something to the plan sketched by a Luxembourg politician in 1970.
The oil crisis of 1973 and the global steel crisis that followed hit Luxembourg hard.
Steel demand collapsed, and the mills in the south were suddenly in danger.
In 1977, rather than let mass unemployment tear society apart, the government brought the unions and the employers together in a standing body, the Tripartite.
They negotiated early retirements, retraining, and state support, avoiding the bitter strikes and layoffs that wrecked other industrial regions in Europe.
This approach of consensus and dialogue became known as the Luxembourg model, and it shaped the country's politics for decades.
Finally, a lighter note. In these same years, Luxembourg quietly became a superpower of pop music.

Radio Luxembourg, broadcasting in English by night on medium wave, was one of the few ways British teenagers could hear the latest records, and many remember listening under their blankets with a transistor radio.
And the Eurovision Song Contest, Luxembourg won five times, in 1961, 1965, 1972, 1973, and 1983.
Among the winners was the French singer France Gall, who won in 1965 with a song written by Serge Gainsbourg.
A country with a few hundred thousand people won more times than many with far larger populations, helped by its commercial radio and its talent for hiring great singers from abroad.
By 1980, the Luxembourg that had been invaded and half-destroyed was a comfortable, cosmopolitan little state, with a seat at Europe's table.
But the steel that had made it rich was in decline.
The question was what would replace it.
And the answer, as we will see, was money.
